clinical_category: Lumbar puncture safety in suspected bacterial meningitis - raised ICP screening
blueprint_topic: Preprocedure risk assessment and prevention of neurologic complications
stem: An adult with suspected bacterial meningitis has a GCS of 8 and a new focal neurologic deficit. A lumbar puncture is being considered. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Notify the team that neuroimaging is indicated and lumbar puncture should be deferred until the raised-ICP risk factors are addressed, while urgent treatment is not delayed
options.B: Proceed directly with lumbar puncture because suspected meningitis always overrides neurologic contraindications
options.C: Delay antibiotics until both neuroimaging and lumbar puncture have been completed
options.D: Assume every client with suspected meningitis requires routine neuroimaging before lumbar puncture even when no contraindication is present

rationale: A is correct. NICE guideline NG240 states that neuroimaging should not be performed routinely before lumbar puncture. However, imaging is indicated when there are risk factors for an evolving space-occupying lesion or signs suggesting raised intracranial pressure, including new focal neurologic features, abnormal pupillary reactions, a GCS of 9 or less, or a progressive fall in consciousness; lumbar puncture should not be performed until these factors are resolved. NICE also directs that blood tests, antibiotics, and stabilization occur before imaging in this situation. Current WHO guidance likewise emphasizes that suspected bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and lumbar puncture should never cause harmful delay in antibiotic treatment. B ignores specific neurologic safety criteria. C dangerously delays treatment. D overuses imaging and contradicts the recommendation against routine pre-LP neuroimaging.
educational_objective: Before lumbar puncture for suspected bacterial meningitis, identify signs of raised intracranial pressure that require imaging and deferral of LP while ensuring urgent antimicrobial treatment and stabilization are not delayed.
source_organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), corroborated by World Health Organization (WHO)
source_document_title: Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease: recognition, diagnosis and management (NG240); WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care
source_version_date: NICE NG240 published 2024-03-19; WHO meningitis guideline published 2025-04-10 and 2026 practical implementation manual current; accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NICE NG240 → Recommendations 1.4.6–1.4.8 and 1.4.9–1.4.12: do not routinely image before LP; image for evolving space-occupying-lesion risk or raised-ICP signs including new focal neurologic features, abnormal pupils, GCS ≤9, or progressive decline; do not perform LP until these factors are resolved; take bloods, give antibiotics, and stabilize before imaging. WHO 2025 meningitis guidance/fact sheet → Diagnosis/Treatment: LP is important for diagnosis but must not delay antibiotic treatment when bacterial meningitis is suspected.
source_claim_supported: Current NICE and WHO guidance directly support selective pre-LP neuroimaging for specified raised-ICP risk features, deferral of LP when those features are present, and avoidance of treatment delay in suspected bacterial meningitis.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential client-needs subcategory (9–15% of items); this item tests preprocedure risk assessment, contraindication recognition, and prevention of complications from diagnostic procedures.
correction_summary: Total safety rebuild. The original generic AANN item implied broad screening for increased ICP and suggested imaging as a generalized prerequisite. The final item uses current NICE criteria to identify exactly when imaging is required before LP, explicitly rejects routine imaging for all suspected meningitis, and preserves the current WHO principle that antimicrobial treatment must not be delayed.
audit_findings: The original generic AANN source did not provide exact current criteria for when neuroimaging should precede lumbar puncture.
NICE NG240 directly identifies new focal neurologic features and GCS ≤9 as signs requiring imaging and deferral of LP until the risk factors are resolved.
The final item explicitly avoids the incorrect universal rule that every suspected meningitis patient needs imaging before LP.
Current WHO guidance supports not delaying antibiotic treatment for lumbar puncture or diagnostic confirmation.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely safe answer, no second defensible option, no unsupported universal contraindication or imaging rule, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
